title: The Built Environment and the Brain: Review of Emerging Methods to Investigate the Impact of Viewing Architectural Design
review_question: To explore methodologies at the intersection of architecture and neuroscience, examining the impact of viewing interior, building, and urban design on neurophysiological mechanisms underlying cognitive, affective, and behavioural responses, and to offer insights for enhancing methodologies and creating environments positively impacting human well-being.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: English peer-reviewed papers were searched in PubMed, ScienceDirect, Nature, Springer, Taylor & Francis, Wiley, and Google Scholar. Search terms included architecture, built environment, indoor space, urban environment, neuroscience, neuroimaging, neuroarchitecture, brain, activity, EEG, fMRI, and NIRS. Bibliographic references of retrieved works were also reviewed. Selection was based on relevance and suitability, spanning years 2005–2023.

findings.antecedent: Architectural representations (real/detailed images vs. simpler sketches)
findings.consequent: Neural processing (episodic memory, visual processing, mental calculation, memory encoding/recognition)
findings.quote: Evidence from EEG studies illustrates distinct neural processing of different representations of architectural environments.

findings.antecedent: Sustainable building interiors (lighting, view, spatial arrangement) vs. conventional interiors
findings.consequent: Cognitive function (visual system engagement, attentional focus, control processing, theta/delta activities, frontal activity), mental health (mindfulness, awareness)
findings.quote: participants exhibited heightened visual system engagement and adjusted their attentional focus and control processing within the sustainable compared to the conventional environment

findings.antecedent: Spatial layout (wide wall location) and window size (broader windows)
findings.consequent: Perceived density, positive affect, mu-rhythm, theta power, early spatial attention
findings.quote: density perception relates to movement planning, suggesting that design parameters such as an expanding space can modulate early spatial attention.

findings.antecedent: Natural views or indoor plants in workplace settings
findings.consequent: Anxiety levels, EEG-b values, EEG-a effects, BVP readings
findings.quote: exposure to natural views or indoor plants reduced anxiety levels, while their absence increased tension and anxiety

findings.antecedent: Indoor vegetation density (optimal range 13%-24%)
findings.consequent: Psychophysiological stress reduction, perceived restorativeness, relative alpha power spectral density (PSD), beta relative PSD, selective visual attention
findings.quote: psychophysiological stress reduction as indoor vegetation increased, peaking at a density range of 13%-24% before plateauing.

findings.antecedent: Curvilinear vs. rectilinear interior spaces (images)
findings.consequent: Perceived beauty, ACC activity (pleasant/rewarding effect)
findings.quote: curvilinear spaces were more likely to be perceived as beautiful, correlating with increased activity in the ACC, indicating a pleasant and rewarding effect of curves

findings.antecedent: Ceiling height (high vs. low) and enclosure (open vs. enclosed spaces) in images
findings.consequent: Perceived beauty, visuospatial processing (left precuneus, left middle gyrus), abstract representations processing (left middle temporal gyrus, right superior temporal gyrus), potential fear response (aMCC activation)
findings.quote: high ceilings were considered more beautiful, activating the left precuneus and left middle gyrus related to visuospatial processing

findings.antecedent: Psychological dimensions (coherence, fascination, hominess) of interior design images, task (beauty judgment vs. approach-avoidance)
findings.consequent: Neural activation patterns (right lingual gyrus, left inferior occipital gyrus, left cuneus)
findings.quote: the valuation of architectural processing in the visual cortices varies by dimension, as well as by task

findings.antecedent: Virtual vs. real classrooms
findings.consequent: Cognitive test accuracy, eye blink rate, heart rate, head acceleration, GSR variance, EEG frequency band-power, ERPs
findings.quote: research has found consistency in the cognitive and neurophysiological responses to virtual compared to real-world environments

findings.antecedent: Virtual residential bedroom interior designs (novelty, pleasantness, comfort, familiarity)
findings.consequent: Mu-rhythm, frontal alpha/theta activity, spatial navigation regions, embodied simulation mechanisms, motivational factors, attention, positive emotion
findings.quote: the cerebral processes underlying the appreciation of architecture involve diverse mechanisms regulating bodily, emotional, and cognitive responses.

findings.antecedent: Virtual transitions with different passability levels (narrow, mid, wide doors)
findings.consequent: Subjective ratings (dominance, arousal, valence), approach times, evoked potentials (frontocentral, occipital sites), motor-related brain activity, prediction error
findings.quote: environmental affordances impact early cortical potentials... even before actual movement

findings.antecedent: Architectural cues (ambiguous/non-ambiguous VEs, signage, interior design elements, colors)
findings.consequent: Spatial orientation and navigation (wayfinding behaviors), brain responses (occipital, parietal, occipitotemporal, frontal areas), theta band synchronization, lower alpha band desynchronization, cognitive engagement, attentional demands
findings.quote: investigations into spatial navigation within virtual environments emphasized the significant impact of architectural cues on spatial orientation and navigation

findings.antecedent: Virtual mazes with varying ceiling heights and objects
findings.consequent: Wayfinding behaviors (directional behavior, object-mapping, recall rates), anxiety-related beta activity
findings.quote: The height of the space affected directional behaviour both cognitively and behaviourally.

findings.antecedent: Relaxing vs. stressful virtual educational spaces (manipulated luminance, daylight, color, openness, visual cues)
findings.consequent: EEG oscillations (theta, alpha, beta), GSR, HRV, self-reported pleasantness, focus, relaxation, stress, anxiety
findings.quote: relaxing versus stressful virtual educational spaces... were found to actually influence stress and anxiety

findings.antecedent: Forms of interior spaces (curved shapes) in virtual environments
findings.consequent: Emotional responses (ACC activation), affective ratings
findings.quote: curved shapes leading to stronger activations and more positive affective ratings

findings.antecedent: Geometrical properties (protrusion, curvature, proportion, scale) in virtual environments
findings.consequent: Emotional effects, cognitive processes, dwell times, liking scores, pupillary diameters, fixation rates/durations, beta ratio, GSR
findings.quote: factors like protrusion, curvature, proportion, and scale having pronounced emotional effects

findings.antecedent: Scale of interior spaces in virtual environments
findings.consequent: SCR, HRV, self-reported emotional states, EEG power (beta, low-gamma, high-gamma), left lateralization (gamma), frontal midline power (theta, alpha), theta connectivity (left temporoparietal, right frontal), high-gamma connectivity (right frontoparietal)
findings.quote: Enlarged scale led to increased EEG power within the beta bandwidth and elevated frontal midline low-gamma and high-gamma power

findings.antecedent: Ceiling height, aspect ratio, and window ratio in virtual postpartum care unit
findings.consequent: Relaxation-arousal responses (RAB waves), brain regions (right frontal, left parietal lobes)
findings.quote: ceiling height, aspect ratio, and window ratio impacted users' relaxation-arousal responses

findings.antecedent: Room width in virtual educational settings
findings.consequent: Cognitive performance, HRV-LFHF metric, EEG-C3-Beta, EEG-CZ-Highbeta, attention, memory
findings.quote: Cognitive performance declined as room width increased.

findings.antecedent: Room width and window location in educational settings
findings.consequent: Cognitive scores, EEG components (theta, alpha), connectivity (centro-parietal to frontal electrodes), short-term memory encoding
findings.quote: characteristics of brain activity during cognitive tasks are influenced by room width as well as window location

findings.antecedent: Window size, aperture designs, and sky type (clear vs. overcast) in virtual workplace environments
findings.consequent: Subjective responses (interest, excitement, complexity, calmness, satisfaction, exterior views, brightness), EEG (beta variations, power, mean theta rhythm), electrocardiogram
findings.quote: Irregular designs were associated with higher interest, excitement, and complexity, while regular designs... with calmness, satisfaction with exterior views, and brightness.

findings.antecedent: Store layout (number of aisles) in virtual grocery stores
findings.consequent: Product recall, cognitive workload, perceived visual complexity, perceived attractiveness, alpha power (ACC), RSC activation, attention, cognitive engagement, decision-making, visual memory, spatial navigation
findings.quote: simpler store layouts might be more effective in terms of consumer responses.

findings.antecedent: Color hues (cold vs. warm) in virtual classrooms
findings.consequent: Error rates (attention task), memory performance, sympathetic activity, parasympathetic activity, brain activations (beta, high-beta bands), arousal, cognitive performance, working memory
findings.quote: Spaces with cold-hues were associated with better error rates in the attention task and higher memory performance.

findings.antecedent: Blue ambient wall color in virtual environments
findings.consequent: Respiration, SCR, HRV, PSD (theta, alpha, beta), frontal alpha midline power, frontal hemispheric lateralization, theta connectivity (frontal region), low-gamma range activity (right occipital region), emotional response, cognitive processes, mental health
findings.quote: Blue colour led to an increased range in respiration and SCR, along with an insignificant drop in mean values of HRV.

findings.antecedent: Artificial lighting (illumination levels, correlated color temperature (CCT)) in virtual office spaces
findings.consequent: EEG band features (frontal, parietal regions), α/θ, β/0, α/β, α/γ ratios, cognitive processing, spatial perception
findings.quote: Higher illumination levels affected activity in the frontal and parietal regions, which are involved in cognitive processing and spatial perception

findings.antecedent: Green walls (small vs. large) in virtual reality
findings.consequent: Self-reported stress, anxiety, EDA, relative alpha power (parietal, occipital lobe), mental stress, mental fatigue, relaxation, arousal
findings.quote: The effectiveness of (small and large) green walls in relieving stress indoors was examined

findings.antecedent: Biophilic elements (plant wall and/or digital wall) in virtual hospital patient rooms
findings.consequent: Low-frequency brainwave activity (relaxation), high-frequency activity (arousal), frontal regions activity, alpha power (frontal), self-reported negative emotions, emotional well-being
findings.quote: Biophilic designs (with plant wall and/or digital wall) led to an increase in low-frequency brainwave activity associated with relaxation

findings.antecedent: Bed orientation (north-south vs. east-west) in real rooms
findings.consequent: Total sleep time, REM latency, slow-wave sleep (SWS) latency, arousals, awakenings, EEG (delta, theta, alpha bands), alpha band energy ratio, sleep quality
findings.quote: sleeping in the north-south direction might be more beneficial than east-west and that sleep EEG signals can be sensitive to Earth's electromagnetic field.

findings.antecedent: Colors (colorful/red/blue/grey) in full-scale rooms
findings.consequent: Brain activity (alpha rhythm, delta waves), mood (activation, extraversion, emotional control, wakefulness, boredom), heart rate, perceived pleasantness, closedness, originality, complexity, coherence, arousal
findings.quote: the profound impact of colour on physiological responses and emotional states in real environments

findings.antecedent: Direct and indirect lighting in real residential living rooms
findings.consequent: Perceived coolness, pleasantness, theta oscillations (right fronto-temporal, left temporo-parietal areas), theta power (right frontal region), emotional status
findings.quote: the combination of direct and indirect lighting enhanced feelings of pleasantness, influencing subjective perceptions of the space.

findings.antecedent: Greenness index for interior spaces (optimal 50%)
findings.consequent: Subjective preference, HRV, cardiac normal-to-normal (NN) intervals, autonomic activity, EEG data (frontopolar, occipital lobes), mean amplitude (left occipital electrode), relaxing effect
findings.quote: even a small amount of greenery may evoke a relaxing effect in a limited space.

findings.antecedent: Interior designs (standard vs. designed) in actual-size rooms
findings.consequent: Subjective responses, parasympathetic activity, sympathetic activity, diastolic blood pressure, regional cerebral blood flow (rCBF) on left frontal area, calm state, active state, familiarity, interest
findings.quote: the standard room with common interiors caused a calm state, which was interpreted to be due to familiarity, while the designed room caused an active state.

findings.antecedent: Abstraction degrees of virtual environments (abstract, semi-designed, fully designed)
findings.consequent: Perceived ease of navigation, creativity, liking, beta2/beta3 bands activity, motor network activation (pre-central gyrus), aesthetic appreciation, embodied simulation
findings.quote: Abstract (compared to designed) environments led to activations in the motor network, especially the pre-central gyrus, suggesting that sensorimotor areas are involved in the aesthetic appreciation of abstract art

findings.antecedent: Architectural decorum (high- vs. low-ranking fictitious buildings)
findings.consequent: Neural responses (ERPs, N400-potentials), familiarity, visual-semantic processing
findings.quote: high-ranking buildings evoke a stronger sense of familiarity.

findings.antecedent: High- vs. low-ranking buildings, TLE patients with/out hippocampal sclerosis and healthy controls
findings.consequent: Early negative potentials (200-400ms), late positive potentials (LPPs) (400-600ms), visual object selection, post-model selection, hippocampus contribution
findings.quote: the distinction between high- and low-ranking buildings involves two key processes: early visual object selection and late post-model selection, underscoring the critical contribution of the hippocampus

findings.antecedent: High- vs. low-ranking buildings, German vs. Chinese participants
findings.consequent: Classification performance, response times, N350 response, late positive components, cultural expertise, object identification
findings.quote: the ability to identify architectural hierarchy is influenced by culturally specific expertise in Western-style architecture

findings.antecedent: Noted-architect-designed vs. ordinary architectures (colored photographs)
findings.consequent: P2 amplitude, N2 amplitude, emotional response, novelty perception, aesthetic evaluation
findings.quote: These findings introduce P2 and N2 as discerning neural markers for assessing the delight and novelty aspects expressed by architectural designs.

findings.antecedent: Window shapes on building facades (rectangular, square, circular, semi-circular arch, triangular, triangular arch)
findings.consequent: Perceived pleasantness, ERP components (N1, P2, P3), brain activity (frontal, posterio-occipital regions), ERP amplitudes (right hemisphere), positive/negative emotions
findings.quote: unpleasant (triangular) shapes generating higher brain activity particularly in frontal and posterio-occipital regions

findings.antecedent: Greenery visible from various floor levels
findings.consequent: Alpha oscillations (frontal cortex), frontal alpha, temporal beta, positive emotional states, motivation, visual attention
findings.quote: increased greenery increases activation in brainwaves associated with positive emotional states, motivation, and visual attention

findings.antecedent: Architecture expertise (experts vs. non-experts) viewing images of objects, faces, houses, and buildings
findings.consequent: Aesthetic judgments, neural activation (mOFC, SCG, NAcc, hippocampus, precuneus), reward processing, memory, integration of prior knowledge
findings.quote: expertise influenced both cognitive processing and responses in brain areas related to reward.

findings.antecedent: Architectural styles (different styles, famous architects' designs, entry-level scenes, faces) in images
findings.consequent: Neural activity patterns (high-level visual brain regions, fusiform face area (FFA)), detailed neural representation of scenes
findings.quote: FFA plays a crucial role in the detailed neural representation of scenes at a subordinate level, specifically buildings' architectural styles.

findings.antecedent: Sharp vs. curved contours in healthcare settings (objects, interiors, exteriors, landscapes)
findings.consequent: Amygdala activation, preference, fear response, precognitive response
findings.quote: Sharp conditions in object and landscape categories led to increased bilateral amygdala activation, indicating a potential fear response.

findings.antecedent: Contemplative vs. ordinary buildings (images)
findings.consequent: Internal states (attentive, receptive, absorbing experiences, reduced internal dialogue), PFC involvement, occipital lobe, precentral gyrus, inferior parietal lobule, medial PFC, hippocampus, cerebellum, default mode network (DMN) engagement, meditative state, self-regulation, executive attention, aesthetic/emotional engagement
findings.quote: contemplative architecture may induce a meditative state by reducing the need for self-regulation and executive attention, thereby enhancing aesthetic and emotional engagement.

findings.antecedent: Pleasant vs. unpleasant places (educational settings) in images
findings.consequent: Brain regions activation (emotion-related regions, amygdala, frontal lobe, occipital lobe, fusiform, middle occipital lobe), affect changes, aesthetic judgment, decision-making
findings.quote: architectural settings may impact emotional, perceptual, cognitive, aesthetic judgment, and decision-making processes

findings.antecedent: Glass floor platforms at varying heights (15-75m) in virtual environments
findings.consequent: Affect scores (depression, tension), stress, anxiety, GSR, HRV, focal points, eye movement speed, alpha waves (prefrontal, occipital lobes), physiological stress
findings.quote: glass floor built to 15–30 m height is appropriate, while neurocognitive and physiological problems seem to appear at 45 m height and above

findings.antecedent: Salient/non-salient target buildings (varying height, footprint, facade pattern) in virtual city routes
findings.consequent: Recall accuracy, gaze duration, spatial awareness (posterior lateral EEG theta power), neural activation (left superior posterior regions), wayfinding, visual attraction of landmarks
findings.quote: building shape and height can influence the visual attraction of landmarks

findings.antecedent: Green vs. concrete facades
findings.consequent: Subjective ratings, negative mood, positive mood, relative alpha wave power (occipital, prefrontal lobe), parasympathetic activity, sympathetic activity, SCR, relaxation, emotional responses, attention, visual perception, brain function
findings.quote: Green façades enhance relaxation compared with concrete walls.

findings.antecedent: Urban environments (urban green, urban outdoor, urban indoor) with different social density (crowded vs. uncrowded), active walking vs. standing
findings.consequent: Perceived calmness, positivity, attentional demands, arousal, negative valence, cognitive demands, frontal alpha asymmetry, EEG signal-to-noise ratio, skin conductance, emotional responses
findings.quote: emotional reactions to visual stimuli can be efficiently assessed using mobile EEG and EDA in mobile settings

findings.antecedent: Natural vs. urban scenes (images)
findings.consequent: Subjective evaluation (restorativeness), arousal, interest, meditation levels, ERPs (P1, N1, EPN, P300, LPP), oscillatory activity (delta, theta, high alpha, beta, low alpha waves), cognitive/attentional demands
findings.quote: natural environments recruit less cognitive and attentional demands

findings.antecedent: Contemplative (CL) vs. non-contemplative (NCL) landscapes (images)
findings.consequent: Frontal alpha asymmetry, frontal beta power, beta power (right temporal regions), visual attention, stress reduction
findings.quote: CL captured more visual attention, supporting the ART... and suggesting a stress reduction mechanism.

findings.antecedent: High restorative potential (HRP) photos (natural environments) vs. low restorative potential (LRP) photos (built environments without nature)
findings.consequent: Brain regions activation (middle frontal gyrus, middle/inferior temporal gyrus, insula, inferior parietal lobe, cuneus, superior frontal gyrus, precuneus, parahippocampal gyrus, posterior cingulate), involuntary/bottom-up attention, top-down/directed attention
findings.quote: HRP environments triggered involuntary, bottom-up attention-related brain regions, while LRP environments engaged areas associated with top-down, directed attention.

findings.antecedent: Urban, mountain, forest, and water scenes (images)
findings.consequent: Perceived restorativeness, brain activity (left/right cuneus, right cingulate gyrus, left precuneus), attention focus, visual/attentional brain areas
findings.quote: Viewing urban as opposed to natural landscapes... increased activations in the visual and attentional brain areas

findings.antecedent: Rural/natural vs. urban residential environments (images)
findings.consequent: Expressed comfort, brain activation (calcarine gyrus, ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, ACC, medial prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, amygdala, insula), visual processing, cognitive control, emotion regulation/expression
findings.quote: An expressed comfort was observed when viewing rural and natural residential environments, contrasting with discomfort felt when observing urban residential scenes.

findings.antecedent: Natural vs. built environments (images), equally rated on scenicness
findings.consequent: Perceived stress, rumination, valence, arousal, dominance, functional connectivity (dorsal attention network (DAN), ventral attention network (VAN), DMN, somatomotor connections)
findings.quote: Functional connectivity was notably greater when participants viewed images of natural landscapes compared to built environments.

findings.antecedent: Green urban landscapes with varying green-space densities (images)
findings.consequent: Brain activations (SPL, STG, PCC, mFG, cuneus), stress-related responses, spatial processing, executive attention, attention restoration
findings.quote: vPCC regulates nature dose-dependent stress changes, potentially through connections to the prefrontal and hippocampal region

findings.antecedent: Natural landscapes and landscape gardens (images)
findings.consequent: Brain regions activation (bilateral middle temporal gyri, right superior temporal gyrus, left superior frontal gyrus, right middle cingulate, left medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC), left precuneus, left rolandic operculum, right ACC, inferior occipital lobe, left SPL, right fusiform gyrus, right cuneus, supplementary motor area), rewarding perception, attentional orienting, visual processing, emotional reward, embodied motivation
findings.quote: landscape gardens elicited increased activation in various brain regions... indicating a rewarding perception.

findings.antecedent: Static vs. dynamic landscapes (images)
findings.consequent: Brain regions activation (occipital lobe, frontal lobe, supplementary motor area, cingulate cortex, insula, middle temporal gyrus (MT/V5), hippocampus), aesthetic judgment, visual processing, emotion-related regions
findings.quote: dynamic landscapes evoked stronger activations in the middle temporal gyrus (MT/V5) and hippocampus, suggesting greater beauty in dynamic stimuli

findings.antecedent: Pleasant vs. less pleasant walking environments (videos from pedestrian perspective)

findings.quote: Viewing pleasant walking environments... was correlated with a decrease in the hemodynamic response in the right and central areas of the PFC, indicating physiological relaxation.

findings.antecedent: Urban vs. garden visuals (images)
findings.consequent: Oxygenated haemoglobin levels (O2Hb) (left/right PFC), mood states, perceived naturalness, comfort, brain activity, negative mood states, calming effect
findings.quote: urban and natural environments elicit distinct brain activations.

findings.antecedent: Urban vs. garden videos
findings.consequent: HbO (right PFC), pleasant/stressful effects
findings.quote: garden scenes may offer more pleasant and less stressful effects than urban scenes.

findings.antecedent: Nature images vs. city scenes
findings.consequent: Mood (comfortableness, relaxation, vigor), oxyhaemoglobin (oxy-Hb) (right OFC), mood-improving effect
findings.quote: the mood-improving effect of viewing images of nature was confirmed by reduced activity in the right OFC

findings.antecedent: Urban/natural scenes before and after Covid-19 lockdown (videos)
findings.consequent: Average Oxy-Hb levels (visual cortex, frontal eye fields), stress, anxiety, brain haemodynamics
findings.quote: haemodynamic patterns associated with stress and anxiety appeared in response to the urban scenes but not in scenes with natural elements

findings.antecedent: Virtual urban environment before and after redesign (building types, natural features, street characteristics, architecture features, front porch, building height)
findings.consequent: Questionnaire scores, emotional reactions (engagement, interest, attention, relaxation, moderate stress levels)
findings.quote: diverse emotional reactions, ranging from negative and positive to neutral, towards the two built environments.

findings.antecedent: Visual patterns of urban streets (spatial scales, proportion of vegetation, fragmentation, diversity) in virtual scenes
findings.consequent: Emotional responses (comfort, vitality, excitement, interest), SCR amplitude, HR, physiological arousal, valence
findings.quote: the proportion of vegetation positively impacted emotional responses, including subjective comfort and vitality.

findings.antecedent: Landmarks in maze-like virtual navigation (landmark-enriched vs. landmark-devoid)
findings.consequent: Performance (better, more efficient), left hemisphere brain activity, theta frequency band event-related desynchronization/synchronization (left posterior inferior/superior regions), cognitive demands, object-location binding, spatial transformation
findings.quote: landmarks facilitated spatial navigation, with EEG analyses showing increased left-hemispheric activation, particularly in the parietal cortex

findings.antecedent: Walking in urban areas (wayfinding decisions, social interactions, crossing streets, familiar vs. new streets)
findings.consequent: Beta activity peaks, theta/alpha range activities, cognitive engagement, curiosity, cognitive load, memory performance
findings.quote: Critical way-finding decisions were marked by short, intense beta activity peaks, supporting link between beta waves and active decision-making.

findings.antecedent: Real-life urban experiences (urban shopping street, green space, busy commercial district) during walking
findings.consequent: Frustration, engagement, arousal, meditation, stress reduction
findings.quote: urban green spaces, in particular, have the potential to reduce stress and promote a meditative state.

findings.antecedent: Different urban environments (café, supermarket, garden)
findings.consequent: Meditation component, alpha waves, beta waves, mental activity
findings.quote: the meditation component showed higher levels in the garden and café compared with the supermarket

findings.antecedent: Urban environment changes (walk from urban busy streets to urban green space) for older adults
findings.consequent: Engagement levels, excitement levels, frustration levels, mood, cognitive load, alpha waves, beta waves, stress, attention, relaxation
findings.quote: The urban green space seemed to exert a restorative effect on this group of older adults

findings.antecedent: Urban green spaces (park, neighbourhood green space, busy urban street) in images
findings.consequent: Frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA), mood, positive mood
findings.quote: Parks, in particular, promoted positive moods, emphasizing the nuanced effects of different green environments on neural states.

findings.antecedent: Street network characteristics (global/local integration) using Space Syntax methodology
findings.consequent: Brain activity during stress provocation (dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, insula, thalamus), detecting salient stimuli/threat
findings.quote: higher levels of global and local integration (better integrated streets) were associated with reduced brain activity during stress provocation.

findings.antecedent: 90-min walk in natural vs. urban environment
findings.consequent: Self-reported rumination, neural activity in subgenual prefrontal cortex (sgPFC), mental well-being
findings.quote: walking in a natural setting decreased self-reported rumination

findings.antecedent: One-hour walk in natural vs. urban environment, followed by fearful faces task and social stress task
findings.consequent: Amygdala activation, stress-related brain areas
findings.quote: amygdala activation decreased after the nature walk while it remained stable after the walk in the urban environment.

findings.antecedent: Walking in urban vs. natural environments (positive sequence: urban to natural; negative sequence: natural to urban)
findings.consequent: HbO2 concentration level, EDA signals, sense of relaxation, sense of interest, emotional scores, emotional health
findings.quote: natural environments elicited higher emotional scores and a stronger sense of relaxation and interest.

synthesis_conclusions: Interior design features are well explored in various settings, but building and urban design research remains relatively underexplored.

There is a crucial need to understand the effects of urban environments beyond their often-proposed detrimental aspects, calling for collaborative efforts in neuroscience, architecture, and urban design.
Virtual environments are extensively studied in interior design, but research on naturalistic environments within this scope is limited.
EEG studies, particularly in virtual environments, show progress, but fMRI research is limited, especially regarding VR integration for high spatial resolution.
NIRS methodologies remain underutilized despite their potential usefulness in naturalistic settings.
Current research has a narrow aesthetic focus, neglecting other aspects like ergonomics, affordances, or functionality.
Most studies rely on short-term exposures, highlighting the necessity for longitudinal research to understand enduring and cumulative influences.
There is a reliance on WEIRD populations, underscoring the need for comprehensive exploration of cultural and interindividual differences.
Much of the existing research is correlational, and there is a recognized need to progress towards establishing causality through rigorous experimental designs and intervention studies.
evidence_gaps: Building and urban design research is relatively underexplored compared to interior design.
A crucial gap exists in understanding the effects of urban environments beyond their often-proposed detrimental effects.
Limited research is dedicated to understanding naturalistic environments within the scope of this research line.
A significant gap persists in fMRI research, especially in relation to interior design, and the use of VR in fMRI investigations has been restricted to navigation research.
NIRS methodologies remain underutilized, despite their major usefulness particularly in naturalistic settings.
Current research has a narrow emphasis on the aesthetic aspect of architectural experience, often neglecting other aspects like ergonomics, affordances, or functionality.
Practical constraints imposed by conventional experimental tools and methods restrict participants' mobility and inhibit naturalistic interaction with architectural environments.
The majority of studies pertain to short-term exposures, emphasizing the necessity for longitudinal studies to comprehensively understand enduring and cumulative influences.
There is a reliance on WEIRD populations, overlooking the challenges posed by cultural and other interindividual differences.
A recognized need to progress from correlations to causality, necessitating rigorous experimental designs and intervention studies.

moderators.effect: Women experienced greater stress and anxiety from glass floors at height; men showed more pronounced O2Hb responses in city environments; amygdala activity decrease after nature walk observed only in women; women exhibited higher interest and lower excitement in virtual urban streets.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Differential physiological and emotional responses to environmental features based on gender.

moderators.effect: Expertise influenced cognitive processing and reward responses for building images; no effect on neural coding of architectural styles in visual cortex; experienced architects showed reduced PFC involvement for contemplative buildings.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Differential neural activation patterns and cognitive processing related to aesthetic judgments and memory.

moderators.effect: Cultural expertise influenced early brain responses to high-ranking buildings (N350 response) but not later semantic and episodic processing.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Culturally specific expertise in Western-style architecture influenced early stages of visual object recognition.

moderators.effect: Older adults showed restorative effects in urban green spaces, with higher engagement levels and fluctuations in excitement, engagement, and frustration during transitions.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Urban green spaces exert a restorative effect on older adults' cognitive and emotional outcomes.

moderators.variable: Mental Health Status (depressed vs. healthy young adults)
moderators.effect: Depressed group showed much more positive results in urban green environments compared to typical urban environments, and did not benefit from walking in typical urban settings.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Green urban fabric has a positive effect on both groups, with a more pronounced benefit for depressed individuals.

limitations: The review deliberately focused on the visual system to streamline the analysis, potentially overlooking multisensory aspects.
The field is in a nascent stage, and many methods, particularly EEG, have been used with limited channels.
Most available research addressed architectural design parameters manipulated separately or in combinations, making it difficult to infer individual effects.
The majority of research was conducted on WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) populations, limiting generalizability across cultures.
Most effects discussed pertain to short-term exposures, highlighting the need for longitudinal studies to understand enduring and cumulative influences.
Much of the existing research relies on correlational relationships, necessitating a shift towards establishing causality through rigorous experimental designs.
Challenges exist with outdoor measurements of online brain signals, especially when using commercial-grade devices for urban design studies.
The uniqueness of each participant's input and variations in exposure timing make it difficult to establish a uniform baseline for interpreting results.
Potential issues related to movement artifacts can complicate the interpretation of neural data, particularly with commercial-grade EEG devices.
There is a narrow emphasis on the aesthetic aspect of architectural experience, often neglecting other aspects like ergonomics, affordances, or functionality.
Practical constraints imposed by conventional experimental tools and methods restrict participants' mobility and inhibit naturalistic interaction with architectural environments.
